The authentication schemes are always defined as a list of classes.  REST framework will attempt to authenticate with each class in the list, and will set
`request.user`
and
`request.auth`
using the return value of the first class that successfully authenticates.

If no class authenticates,
`request.user`

`django.contrib.auth.models.AnonymousUser`
, and
`request.auth`
will be set to
`None`
.

The value of
`request.user`
and
`request.auth`
for unauthenticated requests can be modified using the
`UNAUTHENTICATED_USER`
and
`UNAUTHENTICATED_TOKEN`
settings.

## Django 5.1+LoginRequiredMiddleware¶ {#django-51-loginrequiredmiddleware}

If you're running Django 5.1+ and use the
LoginRequiredMiddleware (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/ref/middleware/#django.contrib.auth.middleware.LoginRequiredMiddleware)
, please note that all views from DRF are opted-out of this middleware.  This is because the authentication in DRF is based on authentication and permissions classes, which may be determined after the middleware has been applied.  Additionally, when the request is not authenticated, the middleware redirects the user to the login page, which is not suitable for API requests, where it's preferable to return a 401 status code.

REST framework offers an equivalent mechanism for DRF views via the global settings,
`DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES`
and
`DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES`
.  They should be changed accordingly if you need to enforce that API requests are logged in.

`# Request will only authenticate if `SessionAuthentication` is in use.request=factory.get('/accounts/django-superstars/')request.user=user
response=view(request)`

If you want to test a request involving the REST framework’s 'Request' object, you’ll need to manually transform it first:

When using

`obtain_auth_token`
view explicitly uses JSON requests and responses, rather than using default renderer and parser classes in your settings.

## API Reference¶ {#api-reference}

### AllowAny¶ {#allowany}

The
`AllowAny`
permission class will allow unrestricted access,
regardless of if the request was authenticated or unauthenticated
.

This permission is not strictly required, since you can achieve the same result by using an empty list or tuple for the permissions setting, but you may find it useful to specify this class because it makes the intention explicit.

### IsAuthenticated¶ {#isauthenticated}

The
`IsAuthenticated`
permission class will deny permission to any unauthenticated user, and allow permission otherwise.

This permission is suitable if you want your API to only be accessible to registered users.

### IsAdminUser¶ {#isadminuser}

The
`IsAdminUser`
permission class will deny permission to any user, unless
`user.is_staff`
is
`True`
in which case permission will be allowed.

This permission is suitable if you want your API to only be accessible to a subset of trusted administrators.

This permission is suitable if you want your API to only be accessible to a subset of trusted administrators.

### IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly¶ {#isauthenticatedorreadonly}

The
`IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly`
will allow authenticated users to perform any request.  Requests for unauthenticated users will only be permitted if the request method is one of the "safe" methods;
`GET`
,
`HEAD`
or
`OPTIONS`
.

This permission is suitable if you want to your API to allow read permissions to anonymous users, and only allow write permissions to authenticated users.

### DjangoModelPermissions¶ {#djangomodelpermissions}

`permission_classes=[permissions.IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly,IsOwnerOrReadOnly]`


Make sure to also import the
`IsOwnerOrReadOnly`
class.


`fromsnippets.permissionsimportIsOwnerOrReadOnly`


Now, if you open a browser again, you find that the 'DELETE' and 'PUT' actions only appear on a snippet instance endpoint if you're logged in as the same user that created the code snippet.

## Authenticating with the API¶ {#authenticating-with-the-api}

Because we now have a set of permissions on the API, we need to authenticate our requests to it if we want to edit any snippets.  We haven't set up any
authentication classes (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/authentication/)
, so the defaults are currently applied, which are
`SessionAuthentication`
and
`BasicAuthentication`
.

When we interact with the API through the web browser, we can login, and the browser session will then provide the required authentication for the requests.

Permission checks are always run at the very start of the view, before any other code is allowed to proceed.  Permission checks will typically use the authentication information in the
`request.user`
and
`request.auth`
properties to determine if the incoming request should be permitted.

Permissions are used to grant or deny access for different classes of users to different parts of the API.

The simplest style of permission would be to allow access to any authenticated user, and deny access to any unauthenticated user. This corresponds to the
`IsAuthenticated`
class in REST framework.

A slightly less strict style of permission would be to allow full access to authenticated users, but allow read-only access to unauthenticated users. This corresponds to the
`IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly`
class in REST framework.

## How permissions are determined¶ {#how-permissions-are-determined}

Permissions in REST framework are always defined as a list of permission classes.

# Permissions - Django REST framework

<https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/permissions>

# Permissions¶ {#permissions}

Authentication or identification by itself is not usually sufficient to gain access to information or code.  For that, the entity requesting access must have authorization.
—
Apple Developer Documentation (https://developer.apple.com/library/mac/#documentation/security/Conceptual/AuthenticationAndAuthorizationGuide/Authorization/Authorization.html)

Together with
authentication (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/authentication/)
and
throttling (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/throttling/)
, permissions determine whether a request should be granted or denied access.

Default:


`['rest_framework.authentication.SessionAuthentication','rest_framework.authentication.BasicAuthentication']`


#### DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES¶ {#default_permission_classes}

A list or tuple of permission classes, that determines the default set of permissions checked at the start of a view. Permission must be granted by every class in the list.

Default:


`['rest_framework.permissions.AllowAny',]`


#### DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES¶ {#default_throttle_classes}

A list or tuple of throttle classes, that determines the default set of throttles checked at the start of a view.

Default:
`[]`

#### DEFAULT_CONTENT_NEGOTIATION_CLASS¶ {#default_content_negotiation_class}

A content negotiation class, that determines how a renderer is selected for the response, given an incoming request.

Default:
`'rest_framework.negotiation.DefaultContentNegotiation'`

#### DEFAULT_SCHEMA_CLASS¶ {#default_schema_class}

A view inspector class that will be used for schema generation.

`ifrequest.methodinpermissions.SAFE_METHODS:# Check permissions for read-only requestelse:# Check permissions for write request`


Note
The instance-level
`has_object_permission`
method will only be called if the view-level
`has_permission`
checks have already passed. Also note that in order for the instance-level checks to run, the view code should explicitly call
`.check_object_permissions(request, obj)`
. If you are using the generic views then this will be handled for you by default. (Function-based views will need to check object permissions explicitly, raising
`PermissionDenied`
on failure.)

### BasicAuthentication¶ {#basicauthentication}

This authentication scheme uses
HTTP Basic Authentication (https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc2617)
, signed against a user's username and password.  Basic authentication is generally only appropriate for testing.

If successfully authenticated,
`BasicAuthentication`
provides the following credentials.

`request.user`
will be a Django
`User`
instance.
`request.auth`
will be
`None`
.

Unauthenticated responses that are denied permission will result in an
`HTTP 401 Unauthorized`
response with an appropriate WWW-Authenticate header.  For example:


`WWW-Authenticate:Basicrealm="api"`

In some circumstances instead of returning
`None`
, you may want to raise an
`AuthenticationFailed`
exception from the
`.authenticate()`
method.

Typically the approach you should take is:

If authentication is not attempted, return
`None`
.  Any other authentication schemes also in use will still be checked.
If authentication is attempted but fails, raise an
`AuthenticationFailed`
exception.  An error response will be returned immediately, regardless of any permissions checks, and without checking any other authentication schemes.

You
may
also override the
`.authenticate_header(self, request)`
method.  If implemented, it should return a string that will be used as the value of the
`WWW-Authenticate`
header in a
`HTTP 401 Unauthorized`
response.

If the
`.authenticate_header()`
method is not overridden, the authentication scheme will return
`HTTP 403 Forbidden`
responses when an unauthenticated request is denied access.

### PageNumberPagination¶ {#pagenumberpagination}

This pagination style accepts a single number page number in the request query parameters.

Request
:


`GET https://api.example.org/accounts/?page=4`


Response
:


`HTTP200OK{"count":1023,"next":"https://api.example.org/accounts/?page=5","previous":"https://api.example.org/accounts/?page=3","results":[…]}`


#### Setup¶ {#setup}

To enable the
`PageNumberPagination`
style globally, use the following configuration, and set the
`PAGE_SIZE`
as desired:


`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS':'rest_framework.pagination.PageNumberPagination','PAGE_SIZE':100}`


On
`GenericAPIView`
subclasses you may also set the
`pagination_class`
attribute to select
`PageNumberPagination`
on a per-view basis.

### LimitOffsetPagination¶ {#limitoffsetpagination}

This pagination style mirrors the syntax used when looking up multiple database records. The client includes both a "limit" and an
"offset" query parameter. The limit indicates the maximum number of items to return, and is equivalent to the
`page_size`
in other styles. The offset indicates the starting position of the query in relation to the complete set of unpaginated items.

Request
:


`GET https://api.example.org/accounts/?limit=100&offset=400`


Response
:


`HTTP200OK{"count":1023,"next":"https://api.example.org/accounts/?limit=100&offset=500","previous":"https://api.example.org/accounts/?limit=100&offset=300","results":[…]}`


#### Setup¶ {#setup_1}

To enable the
`LimitOffsetPagination`
style globally, use the following configuration:


`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS':'rest_framework.pagination.LimitOffsetPagination'}`

`classCustomPagination(pagination.PageNumberPagination):defget_paginated_response(self,data):returnResponse({'links':{'next':self.get_next_link(),'previous':self.get_previous_link()},'count':self.page.paginator.count,'results':data})`


We'd then need to set up the custom class in our configuration:


`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS':'my_project.apps.core.pagination.CustomPagination','PAGE_SIZE':100}`


Note that if you care about how the ordering of keys is displayed in responses in the browsable API you might choose to use an
`OrderedDict`
when constructing the body of paginated responses, but this is optional.

To have your custom pagination class be used by default, use the
`DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS`
setting:


`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS':'my_project.apps.core.pagination.LinkHeaderPagination','PAGE_SIZE':100}`

user_input: Once a list endpoint is paginated, what does the response body actually look like — how is a client supposed to know how many records exist in total and where to get the next batch?
reference: The results get wrapped in an envelope rather than returned as a bare array. A page-number paginated response carries `count` (the total number of records across all pages), `next` and `previous` (full URLs to the adjacent pages, or null at either end), and `results` (the records for this page). Clients walk the collection by following `next` until it comes back null, rather than by computing page numbers themselves.
reference_contexts: HTTP 200 OK { "count": 1023, "next": "https://api.example.org/accounts/?page=5", "previous": "https://api.example.org/accounts/?page=3", "results": [ ... ] }
llm_response:
The structure of a paginated response depends on the pagination style configured.

### Response Body Structure
For the built-in pagination styles, the pagination links and metadata are included directly in the response body. Using `LimitOffsetPagination` as an example, the response body looks like this:

```json
{
    "count": 1023,
    "next": "https://api.example.org/accounts/?limit=100&offset=500",
    "previous": "https://api.example.org/accounts/?limit=100&offset=300",
    "results": [...]
}
```

*   **Total records:** The `count` field indicates the total number of items in the complete set of unpaginated items.
*   **Next batch:** The `next` field provides the URL to retrieve the next page of results.

### Alternative Approaches
*   **Custom Response Bodies:** You can define a custom pagination class to change the structure of the response body. For example, you could nest the links under a specific key:
    ```python
    return Response({
        'links': {
            'next': self.get_next_link(),
            'previous': self.get_previous_link()
        },
        'count': self.page.paginator.count,
        'results': data
    })
    ```
*   **Response Headers:** It is possible to configure pagination to provide links in the response headers (e.g., a `Link` header) instead of the response body. In this case, the pagination links are not included in the body content.

#### New pagination schemes.¶ {#new-pagination-schemes}

Until now, there has only been a single built-in pagination style in REST framework. We now have page, limit/offset and cursor based schemes included by default.

The cursor based pagination scheme is particularly smart, and is a better approach for clients iterating through large or frequently changing result sets. The scheme supports paging against non-unique indexes, by using both cursor and limit/offset information. It also allows for both forward and reverse cursor pagination. user_input: What do I set so clients can search my list endpoint with ?search=?
reference: Add DRF's SearchFilter to the view and give it a search_fields attribute; the filter only activates once search_fields is set.
reference_contexts: When in use, the browsable API will include a SearchFilter control: The SearchFilter class will only be applied if the view has a search_fields attribute set.
The search_fields attribute should be a list of names of text type fields on the model, such as CharField or TextField .
llm_response:
To enable clients to search your list endpoint using `?search=`, you must perform the following steps:

1.  **Add the filter backend:** Include `filters.SearchFilter` in the `filter_backends` attribute of your view.
2.  **Define search fields:** Set the `search_fields` attribute on your view to a list of text-type model fields (e.g., `CharField` or `TextField`) that you want to be searchable.

**Example:**
```python
from rest_framework import filters, generics

class UserListView(generics.ListAPIView):
    queryset = User.objects.all()
    serializer_class = UserSerializer
    filter_backends = [filters.SearchFilter]
    search_fields = ['username', 'email']
```

The `SearchFilter` class will only be applied if the `search_fields` attribute is set. By default, the search parameter is named `'search'`, though this can be overridden using the `SEARCH_PARAM` setting in your `REST_FRAMEWORK` configuration.

## Custom generic filtering¶ {#custom-generic-filtering}

You can also provide your own generic filtering backend, or write an installable app for other developers to use.

To do so override
`BaseFilterBackend`
, and override the
`.filter_queryset(self, request, queryset, view)`
method.  The method should return a new, filtered queryset.

As well as allowing clients to perform searches and filtering, generic filter backends can be useful for restricting which objects should be visible to any given request or user.

### Example¶ {#example}

For example, you might need to restrict users to only being able to see objects they created.


`classIsOwnerFilterBackend(filters.BaseFilterBackend):"""
Filter that only allows users to see their own objects.
"""deffilter_queryset(self,request,queryset,view):returnqueryset.filter(owner=request.user)`

Note
When developing client applications always remember to make sure you're setting the
`Content-Type`
header when sending data in an HTTP request.
If you don't set the content type, most clients will default to using
`'application/x-www-form-urlencoded'`
, which may not be what you want.
As an example, if you are sending
`json`
encoded data using jQuery with the
.ajax() method (https://api.jquery.com/jQuery.ajax/)
, you should make sure to include the
`contentType: 'application/json'`
setting.

## Setting the parsers¶ {#setting-the-parsers}

The default set of parsers may be set globally, using the
`DEFAULT_PARSER_CLASSES`
setting. For example, the following settings would allow only requests with
`JSON`
content, instead of the default of JSON or form data.


`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_PARSER_CLASSES':['rest_framework.parsers.JSONParser',]}`


You can also set the parsers used for an individual view, or viewset,
using the
`APIView`
class-based views.

### Example¶ {#example}

The following class could be used to limit the information that is returned to
`OPTIONS`
requests.


`classMinimalMetadata(BaseMetadata):"""
Don't include field and other information for `OPTIONS` requests.
Just return the name and description.
"""defdetermine_metadata(self,request,view):return{'name':view.get_view_name(),'description':view.get_view_description()}`


Then configure your settings to use this custom class:


`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_METADATA_CLASS':'myproject.apps.core.MinimalMetadata'}`

user_input: How do I let clients order list results but restrict which fields they can sort on?
reference: Use OrderingFilter and set an explicit ordering_fields list on the view so users can't sort on sensitive columns.
reference_contexts: It's recommended that you explicitly specify which fields the API should allow in the ordering filter.
You can do this by setting an ordering_fields attribute on the view, like so: class UserListView ( generics .
llm_response:
To allow clients to order list results while restricting which fields they can sort on, you should use the `OrderingFilter` and explicitly define the allowed fields using the `ordering_fields` attribute on your view.

The documentation recommends this approach to prevent unexpected data leakage, such as allowing users to order by sensitive fields like password hashes.

### Implementation
Include `filters.OrderingFilter` in the `filter_backends` list of your view and set the `ordering_fields` attribute to a list of the specific fields you wish to permit:

```python
from rest_framework import filters, generics

class UserListView(generics.ListAPIView):
    queryset = User.objects.all()
    serializer_class = UserSerializer
    filter_backends = [filters.OrderingFilter]
    ordering_fields = ['username', 'email']
```

### Additional Options
*   **Allowing all fields:** If you are confident the queryset contains no sensitive data, you can set `ordering_fields = '__all__'` to allow ordering on any model field or queryset aggregate.
*   **Default ordering:** You can set an `ordering` attribute on the view to define a default sort order.

The

You can specify custom field-level validation by adding

These methods take a single argument, which is the field value that requires validation.

`serializer=CommentSerializer(data={'email':'foobar','content':'baz'})serializer.is_valid()# Falseserializer.errors# {'email': ['Enter a valid email address.'], 'created': ['This field is required.']}`

`.is_valid()`

`.data`

`.save()`

#### TheBaseSerializerclass.¶ {#the-baseserializer-class}

REST framework now includes a simple
`BaseSerializer`
class that can be used to easily support alternative serialization and deserialization styles.

This class implements the same basic API as the
`Serializer`
class:

`.data`
- Returns the outgoing primitive representation.
`.is_valid()`
- Deserializes and validates incoming data.
`.validated_data`
- Returns the validated incoming data.
`.errors`
- Returns an errors during validation.
`.save()`
- Persists the validated data into an object instance.

There are four methods that can be overridden, depending on what functionality you want the serializer class to support:

#### Usingserializers.ValidationError.¶ {#using-serializersvalidationerror}

Previously
`serializers.ValidationError`
error was simply a synonym for
`django.core.exceptions.ValidationError`
. This has now been altered so that it inherits from the standard
`APIException`
base class.

The reason behind this is that Django's
`ValidationError`
class is intended for use with HTML forms and its API makes using it slightly awkward with nested validation errors that can occur in serializers.

For most users this change shouldn't require any updates to your codebase, but it is worth ensuring that whenever raising validation errors you should prefer using the
`serializers.ValidationError`
exception class, and not Django's built-in exception.

We strongly recommend that you use the namespaced import style of
`import serializers`
and not
`from serializers import ValidationError`
in order to avoid any potential confusion.

#### Change tovalidate_<field_name>.¶ {#change-to-validate_field_name}

user_input: Where do I put validation for a single serializer field?
reference: Add a .validate_<field_name> method to your Serializer subclass — it works like Django forms' .clean_<field_name> and gets the field value.
reference_contexts: You can specify custom field-level validation by adding .validate_<field_name> methods to your Serializer subclass.
llm_response:
You can validate a single serializer field using one of the following two approaches:

*   **Field-level validators:** You can include validators directly on the field instance by declaring them in the `validators` argument when defining the field.
    ```python
    slug = SlugField(max_length=100, validators=[UniqueValidator(queryset=BlogPost.objects.all())])
    ```

*   **`validate_<field_name>` methods:** You can add a method to your `Serializer` subclass named `validate_<field_name>`. This method takes the field value as an argument, must return the validated value, or raise a `serializers.ValidationError`.
    ```python
    def validate_title(self, value):
        if 'django' not in value.lower():
            raise serializers.ValidationError("Blog post is not about Django")
        return value
    ```
    Note that if the field is declared with `required=False`, this validation step will not occur if the field is not included in the input.

When applying an update to an existing instance, uniqueness validators will
exclude the current instance from the uniqueness check. The current instance
is available in the context of the uniqueness check, because it exists as

`instance=...`
when instantiating the serializer.

The validator should be applied to
serializer classes

`UniqueTogetherValidator`

user_input: What's a SerializerMethodField for?
reference: A read-only field whose value comes from a method on the serializer, letting you add arbitrary computed data to the output.
reference_contexts: This is a read-only field. It gets its value by calling a method on the serializer class it is attached to.
llm_response:
A `SerializerMethodField` is a read-only field used to add any sort of data to the serialized representation of an object. It obtains its value by calling a method on the serializer class to which it is attached.

**How to use it:**
*   **Method definition:** The serializer method must accept a single argument (in addition to `self`), which is the object being serialized. It should return the value you want included in the serialized output.
*   **Naming:** By default, the field calls a method named `get_<field_name>`. 
*   **Custom naming:** You can specify a different method name using the `method_name` argument (e.g., `SerializerMethodField(method_name='my_method')`). 
*   **Constraint:** You must not provide a `method_name` argument that matches the default `get_<field_name>` pattern, as this will raise an assertion error.
llm_references:
Signature
:
`SerializerMethodField(method_name=None)`

`method_name`
- The name of the method on the serializer to be called. If not included this defaults to
`get_<field_name>`
.

The serializer method referred to by the
`method_name`
argument should accept a single argument (in addition to
`self`
), which is the object being serialized. It should return whatever you want to be included in the serialized representation of the object. For example:


`fromdjango.contrib.auth.modelsimportUserfromdjango.utils.timezoneimportnowfromrest_frameworkimportserializersclassUserSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):days_since_joined=serializers.SerializerMethodField()classMeta:model=Userfields='__all__'defget_days_since_joined(self,obj):return(now()-obj.date_joined).days`

## Serializer fields¶ {#serializer-fields}

#### TheFieldandReadOnlyfield classes.¶ {#the-field-and-readonly-field-classes}

There are some minor tweaks to the field base classes.

Previously we had these two base classes:

`Field`
as the base class for read-only fields. A default implementation was included for serializing data.
`WritableField`
as the base class for read-write fields.

We now use the following:

`Field`
is the base class for all fields. It does not include any default implementation for either serializing or deserializing data.
`ReadOnlyField`
is a concrete implementation for read-only fields that simply returns the attribute value without modification.

#### Therequired,allow_null,allow_blankanddefaultarguments.¶ {#the-required-allow_null-allow_blank-and-default-arguments}

REST framework now has more explicit and clear control over validating empty values for fields.

The
`queryset`
argument is only ever required for writable fields, and is not required or valid for fields with
`read_only=True`
.

#### Optional argument toSerializerMethodField.¶ {#optional-argument-to-serializermethodfield}

The argument to
`SerializerMethodField`
is now optional, and defaults to
`get_<field_name>`
. For example the following is valid:


`classAccountSerializer(serializers.Serializer):# `method_name='get_billing_details'` by default.billing_details=serializers.SerializerMethodField()defget_billing_details(self,account):returncalculate_billing(account)`


In order to ensure a consistent code style an assertion error will be raised if you include a redundant method name argument that matches the default method name. For example, the following code
will raise an error
:


`billing_details=serializers.SerializerMethodField('get_billing_details')`


#### Enforcing consistentsourceusage.¶ {#enforcing-consistent-source-usage}

#### Example¶ {#example}

For example, if you wanted to be able to set which fields should be used by a serializer at the point of initializing it, you could create a serializer class like so:


`classDynamicFieldsModelSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):"""
A ModelSerializer that takes an additional `fields` argument that
controls which fields should be displayed.
"""def__init__(self,*args,**kwargs):# Don't pass the 'fields' arg up to the superclassfields=kwargs.pop('fields',None)# Instantiate the superclass normallysuper().__init__(*args,**kwargs)iffieldsisnotNone:# Drop any fields that are not specified in the `fields` argument.allowed=set(fields)existing=set(self.fields)forfield_nameinexisting-allowed:self.fields.pop(field_name)`


This would then allow you to do the following:

`>>>serializer=MyComplexModelSerializer()>>>print(serializer)classMyComplexModelSerializer:my_fields=...`


Also keep in mind that with complex cases it can often be better to explicitly
define your serializer classes, rather than relying on the default
`ModelSerializer`
behavior. This involves a little more code, but ensures
that the resulting behavior is more transparent.

With

user_input: How does the source argument on a serializer field work?
reference: source names the attribute used to populate the field; it can be a no-arg method or a dotted path like 'user.email' to traverse relations.
reference_contexts: The name of the attribute that will be used to populate the field.
llm_response:
The `source` argument controls which attribute is used to populate a serializer field. It can point to any attribute on the serialized instance.

### How it works:
*   **Attribute Traversal:** You can use dotted notation (e.g., `source="owner.username"`) to traverse attributes, similar to Django's template language.
*   **Passing the Entire Object:** Using `source='*'` indicates that the entire object should be passed to the field. This is useful for nested representations or when a field requires access to the complete object to determine its output.
*   **Defaults:** By default, the `source` argument is set to the name of the field.

### Important Considerations:
*   **Redundancy:** Explicitly setting `source` to the same value as the field name is redundant and will raise an error.
*   **Performance:** When using dotted notation to access relational ORM models, be aware of potential N+1 problems. It is recommended to use `prefetch_related` or `select_related` to ensure the necessary objects are fetched from the database.
*   **Missing Data:** When using dotted notation, you may need to provide a `default` value if an object is empty or not present during traversal.

## Custom relational fields¶ {#custom-relational-fields}

In rare cases where none of the existing relational styles fit the representation you need,
you can implement a completely custom relational field, that describes exactly how the
output representation should be generated from the model instance.

To implement a custom relational field, you should override
`RelatedField`
, and implement the
`.to_representation(self, value)`
method. This method takes the target of the field as the
`value`
argument, and should return the representation that should be used to serialize the target. The
`value`
argument will typically be a model instance.

If you want to implement a read-write relational field, you must also implement the
.to_internal_value(self, data) method (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/serializers/#to_internal_valueself-data)
.

### SlugRelatedField¶ {#slugrelatedfield}

`SlugRelatedField`
may be used to represent the target of the relationship using a field on the target.

For example, the following serializer:


`classAlbumSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):tracks=serializers.SlugRelatedField(many=True,read_only=True,slug_field='title')classMeta:model=Albumfields=['album_name','artist','tracks']`


Would serialize to a representation like this:


`{'album_name':'Dear John','artist':'Loney Dear','tracks':['Airport Surroundings','Everything Turns to You','I Was Only Going Out',...]}`


By default this field is read-write, although you can change this behavior using the
`read_only`
flag.

When using
`SlugRelatedField`
as a read-write field, you will normally want to ensure that the slug field corresponds to a model field with
`unique=True`
.

Arguments
:

user_input: How do I represent a relation by a unique field on the related object instead of its PK?
reference: Use SlugRelatedField and set slug_field to the attribute you want to represent it by.
reference_contexts: SlugRelatedField may be used to represent the target of the relationship using a field on the target.
llm_response:
To represent a relation using a unique field on the related object instead of its primary key, you should use `SlugRelatedField`.

You can implement this by setting the `slug_field` argument to the name of the field on the target model that you wish to use for representation. When using this as a read-write field, you should ensure the chosen field has `unique=True` set on the model.

Example usage:
```python
class AlbumSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    tracks = serializers.SlugRelatedField(
        many=True, 
        read_only=True, 
        slug_field='title'
    )
    class Meta:
        model = Album
        fields = ['album_name', 'artist', 'tracks']
```

**Required arguments for `SlugRelatedField`:**
*   `slug_field`: The field on the target that should be used to represent it.
*   `queryset`: Required for model instance lookups when validating input (unless `read_only=True` is set).

**Optional arguments:**
*   `many`: Set to `True` if applied to a to-many relationship.
*   `allow_null`: Set to `True` to accept `None` or empty strings for nullable relationships.
*   `read_only`: Used to change the default read-write behavior.

# Parsers¶ {#parsers}

Machine interacting web services tend to use more
structured formats for sending data than form-encoded, since they're
sending more complex data than simple forms
— Malcom Tredinnick,
Django developers group (https://groups.google.com/d/topic/django-developers/dxI4qVzrBY4/discussion)

REST framework includes a number of built-in Parser classes, that allow you to accept requests with various media types.  There is also support for defining your own custom parsers, which gives you the flexibility to design the media types that your API accepts.

## How the parser is determined¶ {#how-the-parser-is-determined}

The set of valid parsers for a view is always defined as a list of classes.  When
`request.data`
is accessed, REST framework will examine the

### Using `APIClient`
If you want to bypass authentication for all requests made by the test client, use the `force_authenticate` method on the `APIClient` instance:

```python
client = APIClient()
client.force_authenticate(user=user)
```

```python
client.force_authenticate(user=None)
```

```python
from rest_framework.test import force_authenticate

factory = APIRequestFactory()
request = factory.get('/accounts/django-superstars/')
force_authenticate(request, user=user)
```
The signature for this method is `force_authenticate(request, user=None, token=None)`. You can set either or both the user and the token. For example:

```python

```

user_input: What's DRF's reverse() and how does it differ from Django's?
reference: rest_framework.reverse.reverse behaves like django.urls.reverse but returns a fully qualified URL using the request's host/port — so pass the request.
reference_contexts: Signature: reverse(viewname, *args, **kwargs) Has the same behavior as django.urls.reverse , except that it returns a fully qualified URL, using the request to determine the host and port.
llm_response:
DRF's `reverse()` is a utility function used to return fully qualified URIs for a Web API, which allows the self-describing API to automatically hyperlink its output.

It differs from Django's `django.urls.reverse` in the following ways:

*   **Fully qualified URLs:** Unlike Django's `reverse`, which returns a path, DRF's `reverse` returns a fully qualified URL by using the request to determine the host and port.
*   **Request requirement:** You should include the `request` as a keyword argument to the function.
*   **Versioning:** DRF's `reverse` ties in with the API's versioning scheme, applying URL transformations appropriate to the current request version (e.g., prepending a namespace or adding a query parameter).

To use it, you import it from `rest_framework.reverse` and pass the view name, arguments, and the `request` object:

```python
from rest_framework.reverse import reverse
reverse('view-name', request=request)
```

There's no requirement for you to use them, but if you do then the self-describing API will be able to automatically hyperlink its output for you, which makes browsing the API much easier.

The `@api_view` decorator performs the following actions on a plain function view:

*   **Request/Response Handling:** It ensures the view receives REST framework `Request` instances instead of Django `HttpRequest` instances and allows the view to return REST framework `Response` objects. It adds context to `Response` objects to enable content negotiation and manages the setting of the correct renderer.
*   **Method Restrictions:** It restricts the view to specific HTTP methods (defaulting to `GET`). If an unsupported method is used, it returns a `405 Method Not Allowed` response.
*   **Exception Handling:** It handles `ParseError` exceptions that occur when accessing `request.data` with malformed input.
*   **Configuration:** It uses the default renderers, parsers, and authentication classes specified in the settings. It also ensures the `.authenticators` property is automatically set based on the view's `authentication_classes` or the `DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATORS` setting.

### GenericAPIView¶ {#genericapiview}

This class extends REST framework's
`APIView`
class, adding commonly required behavior for standard list and detail views.

Each of the concrete generic views provided is built by combining
`GenericAPIView`
, with one or more mixin classes.

#### Attributes¶ {#attributes}

Basic settings
:

The following attributes control the basic view behavior.

Using the
`APIView`
class is pretty much the same as using a regular
`View`
class, as usual, the incoming request is dispatched to an appropriate handler method such as
`.get()`
or
`.post()`
.  Additionally, a number of attributes may be set on the class that control various aspects of the API policy.

For example:


`fromrest_framework.viewsimportAPIViewfromrest_framework.responseimportResponsefromrest_frameworkimportauthentication,permissionsfromdjango.contrib.auth.modelsimportUserclassListUsers(APIView):"""

* Requires token authentication.

"""authentication_classes=[authentication.TokenAuthentication]permission_classes=[permissions.IsAdminUser]defget(self,request,format=None):"""

"""usernames=[user.usernameforuserinUser.objects.all()]returnResponse(usernames)`

REST framework provides an
`APIView`
class, which subclasses Django's
`View`
class.

`APIView`
classes are different from regular
`View`
classes in the following ways:

Requests passed to the handler methods will be REST framework's
`Request`
instances, not Django's
`HttpRequest`
instances.
Handler methods may return REST framework's
`Response`
, instead of Django's
`HttpResponse`
.  The view will manage content negotiation and setting the correct renderer on the response.
Any
`APIException`
exceptions will be caught and mediated into appropriate responses.
Incoming requests will be authenticated and appropriate permission and/or throttle checks will be run before dispatching the request to the handler method.

The generic views provided by REST framework allow you to quickly build API views that map closely to your database models.

If the generic views don't suit the needs of your API, you can drop down to using the regular
`APIView`
class, or reuse the mixins and base classes used by the generic views to compose your own set of reusable generic views.

llm_response:
The DRF-native approach for token-based authentication in mobile clients is `TokenAuthentication`.

### Installation and Configuration
1.  **Add to `INSTALLED_APPS`**: Include `'rest_framework.authtoken'` in your `INSTALLED_APPS` setting.
2.  **Run Migrations**: Execute `python manage.py migrate` to create the necessary database tables for the tokens.
3.  **Configure Authentication**: Configure your authentication classes to include `TokenAuthentication`.

### Obtaining and Using Credentials
*   **Generating Tokens**: You must create tokens for your users. You can do this programmatically:

llm_response:
To structure your API so that everyone can browse data, but only the creator can update or delete it, you should follow these steps:

### 1. Associate records with a creator
Add a field to your model to represent the user who created the record. When saving the instance in your view, use the `perform_create` method to associate the current user with the record:

```python
def perform_create(self, serializer):
    serializer.save(owner=self.request.user)
```

### 2. Implement object-level permissions
Use `permission_classes` to restrict update and delete actions. While the documentation notes that generic views check object-level permissions for single instances (retrieve, update, partial_update, destroy), you must implement a custom permission class that checks if the `request.user` is the owner of the object.

### 3. Ensure read access for everyone
Since you want everyone to be able to browse the data, ensure your global permission policy allows read access (e.g., `AllowAny` or `IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly`). 

### 4. Handle list views
Generic views do not automatically apply object-level permissions to each instance in a list for performance reasons. To ensure users only see what they are permitted to view, you must filter the `queryset` separately in your view.

### Summary of constraints:
* **Creation:** Because `has_object_permission()` is not called when creating objects, you must implement the permission check in your serializer or override the `perform_create()` method in your ViewSet.
* **Read-only fields:** If you need to represent the creator on the serializer without allowing the user to edit it, you can use `serializers.PrimaryKeyRelatedField(read_only=True, default=serializers.CurrentUserDefault())`. Note that as of version 3.8.0, `read_only` fields are excluded from writable fields, so you should pass the owner during `serializer.save()` in `perform_create` as shown above.

llm_response:
To cap requests for anonymous and logged-in users, you should use the `AnonRateThrottle` and `UserRateThrottle` classes.

### Mechanism
*   **`AnonRateThrottle`**: Used to restrict requests from unknown sources. It uses the IP address of the incoming request to generate a unique key.
*   **`UserRateThrottle`**: Used for global rate restrictions per-user. It uses the user ID to generate a unique key, falling back to the IP address for unauthenticated requests.

You can include both in your `DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES` setting to apply them to your API.

### Where the numbers go
The request rates are defined in your Django settings under the `REST_FRAMEWORK` dictionary in the `DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES` setting. You must provide values for the keys `'anon'` and `'user'`:

```python
REST_FRAMEWORK = {
    'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES': [
        'rest_framework.throttling.AnonRateThrottle',
        'rest_framework.throttling.UserRateThrottle',
    ],
    'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES': {
        'anon': '100/day',
        'user': '1000/day'
    }
}
```

Alternatively, you can override the `rate` property directly on a subclass of `AnonRateThrottle` or `UserRateThrottle` if you prefer not to use the global settings.

## Custom throttles¶ {#custom-throttles}

To create a custom throttle, override

`False`

`None`

`.wait()`

`.allow_request()`
has previously returned
`False`
.

Multiple throttles can also be used if you want to impose both burst throttling rates, and sustained throttling rates.  For example, you might want to limit a user to a maximum of 60 requests per minute, and 1000 requests per day.

Throttles do not necessarily only refer to rate-limiting requests.  For example a storage service might also need to throttle against bandwidth, and a paid data service might want to throttle against a certain number of a records being accessed.

The application-level throttling that REST framework provides should not be considered a security measure or protection against brute forcing or denial-of-service attacks. Deliberately malicious actors will always be able to spoof IP origins. In addition to this, the built-in throttling implementations are implemented using Django's cache framework, and use non-atomic operations to determine the request rate, which may sometimes result in some fuzziness.

reference: Yes — stack two throttles instead of picking one number. Yes, you can enforce both burst and sustained throttling rates simultaneously by using multiple throttles.

To implement this, you must override `UserRateThrottle` to create separate classes for each rate and assign them a unique "scope".

**Implementation steps:**

1.  **Define the throttle classes:**
    ```python
    class BurstRateThrottle(UserRateThrottle):
        scope = 'burst'

    class SustainedRateThrottle(UserRateThrottle):
        scope = 'sustained'
    ```

2.  **Configure the settings:**
    Add both classes to your `DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES` and define the rates for each scope in `DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES`:
    ```python
    REST_FRAMEWORK = {
        'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES': [
            'example.throttles.BurstRateThrottle',
            'example.throttles.SustainedRateThrottle'
        ],
        'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES': {
            'burst': '60/min',
            'sustained': '1000/day'
        }
    }
    ```

**Important considerations:**
*   **Limitations:** These throttles are not a security measure against malicious actors, who can spoof IP origins.
*   **Concurrency:** The built-in implementations use non-atomic operations and are open to race conditions, which may allow a few extra requests through under high concurrency. If you require strict guarantees, you must implement a custom throttle class by overriding `BaseThrottle`.

llm_response:
To define a consistent, machine-readable error response across your API without modifying individual views, you should write a custom exception handler. This allows you to intercept exceptions and format the response globally.

You can implement this by creating a function that calls the default `exception_handler` and then modifies the response object. For example:

```python
from rest_framework.views import exception_handler

def custom_exception_handler(exc, context):
    # Call REST framework's default exception handler first
    response = exception_handler(exc, context)

    # If the exception is handled, customize the response data
    if response is not None:
        response.data['detail'] = 'try again shortly'
        # You can also set specific status codes here if needed
        
    return response
```

By using this approach, you avoid writing try/except blocks in every view, as the framework will route exceptions through this handler automatically. 

Note that if `DEBUG=True`, Django's standard traceback error page will be displayed instead of your custom response. Additionally, ensure your application is configured to use this custom handler.

reference: You don't need a second serializer class — the field set is mutable at runtime. Once a serializer is initialized its fields are available as the `.fields` attribute, an ordinary dictionary you can read and modify, which lets you change what gets rendered (and the arguments on individual fields) per instance rather than at declaration time. The documented pattern is a DynamicFieldsModelSerializer: accept an extra `fields` keyword in __init__, pop it before calling super(), and then drop everything not requested from self.fields. Your view decides what to pass — typically driven by a query parameter — so UserSerializer(user) returns the full record and UserSerializer(user, fields=('id', 'email')) returns the narrow one from the same class and the same URL. If you'd rather not hand-roll it, drf-dynamic-fields provides a mixin that limits fields from a URL parameter, and drf-flex-fields additionally handles expanding primitive fields into nested ones.
reference_contexts: Once a serializer has been initialized, the dictionary of fields that are set on the serializer may be accessed using the .fields attribute. Accessing and modifying this attribute allows you to dynamically modify the serializer.
Modifying the fields argument directly allows you to do interesting things such as changing the arguments on serializer fields at runtime, rather than at the point of declaring the serializer.

class DynamicFieldsModelSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer): """ A ModelSerializer that takes an additional `fields` argument that controls which fields should be displayed. """ def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs): # Don't pass the 'fields' arg up to the superclass fields = kwargs.pop('fields', None) # Instantiate the superclass normally super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
print(UserSerializer(user)) {'id': 2, 'username': 'jonwatts', 'email': 'jon@example.com'} print(UserSerializer(user, fields=('id', 'email'))) {'id': 2, 'email': 'jon@example.com'}
The drf-dynamic-fields package provides a mixin to dynamically limit the fields per serializer to a subset specified by an URL parameter.

### Browsability¶ {#browsability}

Because the API chooses the content type of the response based on the client request, it will, by default, return an HTML-formatted representation of the resource when that resource is requested by a web browser.  This allows for the API to return a fully web-browsable HTML representation.

Having a web-browsable API is a huge usability win, and makes developing and using your API much easier.  It also dramatically lowers the barrier-to-entry for other developers wanting to inspect and work with your API.

See the
browsable api (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/topics/browsable-api/)
topic for more information about the browsable API feature and how to customize it.

llm_response:
To cut the boilerplate of writing individual URL patterns for list and detail views, you should use **ViewSets** and a **Router**.

Using `ViewSets` allows you to group common behavior into a single class, which is more concise than writing multiple individual views [5]. Once you have defined your `ViewSet`, you can use a router class to automatically generate the URL configuration for your API [5].

### Implementation
1.  **Register the ViewSet:** In your `urls.py`, import `routers` from `rest_framework` and instantiate a `DefaultRouter`. Register your viewsets with the router:
    ```python
    from rest_framework import routers
    from my_app import views

    router = routers.DefaultRouter()
    router.register(r"users", views.UserViewSet)
    ```

2.  **Include the Router URLs:** Add the router's generated URLs to your `urlpatterns`:
    ```python
    urlpatterns = [
        path("", include(router.urls)),
    ]
    ```

### Notes on `basename`
Typically, you do not need to specify a `basename` argument when registering a viewset. However, if your viewset defines a custom `get_queryset` method and does not have a `.queryset` attribute, the router will be unable to determine the name automatically. In that case, you must explicitly provide the `basename` argument during registration [4].

## Using mixins¶ {#using-mixins}

One of the big wins of using class-based views is that it allows us to easily compose reusable bits of behavior.

The create/retrieve/update/delete operations that we've been using so far are going to be pretty similar for any model-backed API views we create.  Those bits of common behavior are implemented in REST framework's mixin classes.

Note that if you wanted to use this style together with the generic views then you'd also need to override
`.get_object`
on the view in order to get the correct lookup behavior.

Generally we recommend a flat style for API representations where possible, but the nested URL style can also be reasonable when used in moderation.

To address the performance issues caused by rendering a large number of items in the browsable API, you have the following options:

**1. Replace the select input with a text input (Recommended)**
The simplest option for handling a large number of items is to replace the select widget with a standard text input. You can do this by setting the `base_template` style on the field:

```python
author = serializers.HyperlinkedRelatedField(
    queryset=User.objects.all(), 
    style={'base_template': 'input.html'}
)
```

**2. Rely on the default select field cutoff**
The browsable API has a built-in mechanism to prevent performance issues when rendering relational fields. By default, it will only display a maximum of 1000 selectable items. If your lookup table contains more than 1000 items, the system will automatically display a disabled option labeled "More than 1000 items…" instead of attempting to render the entire list. You can control this behavior using two keyword arguments (though the specific names of these arguments are not provided in the excerpts).

To support versioning in your API, you must first enable a versioning scheme. You can do this globally by setting the `DEFAULT_VERSIONING_CLASS` in your `REST_FRAMEWORK` settings, or on an individual view by setting the `versioning_class` attribute.

Once enabled, the `request.version` attribute will contain the version string from the incoming request. You can use this attribute to vary the behavior of your view. For example, you can switch serialization styles by overriding the `get_serializer_class` method:

```python
def get_serializer_class(self):
    if self.request.version == 'v1':
        return AccountSerializerVersion1
    return AccountSerializer
```

Additionally, to ensure that URLs generated by the API (such as those in hyperlinked serializers or via the `reverse` function) correctly reflect the requested version:

*   **For `reverse`:** You must include the current `request` as a keyword argument: `reverse('bookings-list', request=request)`.
*   **For hyperlinked serializers:** You must include the `request` in the serializer context: `serializer = BookingsSerializer(queryset, many=True, context={'request': request})`.

# Versioning¶ {#versioning}

Versioning an interface is just a "polite" way to kill deployed clients.
—
Roy Fielding (https://www.slideshare.net/evolve_conference/201308-fielding-evolve/31)
.

API versioning allows you to alter behavior between different clients. REST framework provides for a number of different versioning schemes.

Versioning is determined by the incoming client request, and may either be based on the request URL, or based on the request headers.

There are a number of valid approaches to approaching versioning.
Non-versioned systems can also be appropriate (https://www.infoq.com/articles/roy-fielding-on-versioning)
, particularly if you're engineering for very long-term systems with multiple clients outside of your control.

To expose a custom action like 'highlight' on a viewset so that the router handles the routing for you, use the `@action` decorator on the method within your `ViewSet`.

### Steps to implement:
1.  **Decorate the method:** Use the `@action` decorator on your method.
2.  **Specify the scope:** Set the `detail` argument to `True` if the action operates on a single instance (e.g., `/snippets/{pk}/highlight/`) or `False` if it operates on the entire collection.
3.  **Configure HTTP methods:** By default, the action will respond to `GET` requests. If you need a different method, use the `methods` argument (e.g., `methods=['post']`).
4.  **Customize the URL (optional):** By default, the URL path is based on the method name. You can override this by providing a `url_path` argument to the decorator.

**Example:**
```python
from rest_framework.decorators import action

class SnippetViewSet(viewsets.ModelViewSet):
    ...
    @action(detail=True)
    def highlight(self, request, pk=None):
        ...
```

Once the method is decorated, register your `ViewSet` with a router (such as `DefaultRouter`), and the router will automatically configure the URL patterns for the extra action.

llm_response:
To render endpoints as real HTML pages using your own templates, you should use the **`TemplateHTMLRenderer`**.

### How it works:
*   **View Return:** The view returns a `Response` object containing a context dictionary. 
*   **Requirements:** You must specify a `template_name` attribute on the view or pass it as an argument to the `Response` object. Unlike other renderers, it does not require serialization of the data.

**Example:**
```python
class ProfileList(APIView):
    renderer_classes = [TemplateHTMLRenderer]
    template_name = 'profile_list.html'

    def get(self, request):
        queryset = Profile.objects.all()
        return Response({'profiles': queryset})
```

### Alternative:
If you are dealing with pre-rendered HTML (a string representing the content) rather than using templates, you should use the **`StaticHTMLRenderer`**. In this case, the view returns a `Response` object containing the HTML string directly.

llm_response:
To accept a raw file upload from a native client, you should use the `FileUploadParser`. Because its `media_type` matches any content type, it should generally be the only parser set on your API view.

### Setting up the parser
Set the `parser_classes` attribute on your view to `[FileUploadParser]`. The uploaded file will be available in `request.data` under the key `'file'`.

```python
from rest_framework.parsers import FileUploadParser
from rest_framework.views import APIView

class FileUploadView(APIView):
    parser_classes = [FileUploadParser]

    def put(self, request, *args, **kwargs):
        file_obj = request.data['file']
        # ...
```

### How DRF gets the filename
DRF determines the filename using one of two methods:

1.  **URL Keyword Argument:** If the view is called with a `filename` URL keyword argument, that argument is used as the filename.
    *   *Example URL configuration:* `re_path(r'^upload/(?P<filename>[^/]+)$', FileUploadView.as_view())`
2.  **Content-Disposition Header:** If no `filename` URL keyword argument is provided, the client must set the filename in the `Content-Disposition` HTTP header.
    *   *Example header:* `Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=upload.jpg`

user_input: I want to combine two permission rules — e.g. authenticated OR a read-only request — without writing a whole new class. Is there a concise way?
reference: Yes: permission classes inheriting from BasePermission compose with Python's bitwise operators, so IsAuthenticated | ReadOnly works using &, | and ~.
reference_contexts: Provided they inherit from rest_framework.permissions.BasePermission , permissions can be composed using standard Python bitwise operators.

method in SAFE_METHODS class ExampleView ( APIView ): permission_classes = [ IsAuthenticated | ReadOnly ] def get ( self , request , format = None ): content = { 'status' : 'request was permitted' } return Response ( content ) Note Composition of permissions supports the & (and), | (or) and ~ (not) operators, and also allows the use of brackets ( ) to group expressions.
Operators follow the same precedence and associativity rules as standard logical operators ( ~ highest, then & , then | ).
llm_response:
Yes, you can combine permission rules using the `|` (or), `&` (and), and `~` (not) operators. This allows you to compose expressions directly within the `permission_classes` list without writing a new class.

For example, to combine `IsAuthenticated` and a custom `ReadOnly` permission, you can use:

```python
permission_classes = [IsAuthenticated | ReadOnly]
```

These operators support the use of brackets `()` to group expressions and follow standard logical operator precedence (highest to lowest: `~`, `&`, `|`).

`IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly`

`HEAD`

Because we now have a set of permissions on the API, we need to authenticate our requests to it if we want to edit any snippets.  We haven't set up any

### AllowAny¶ {#allowany}

The
`AllowAny`
permission class will allow unrestricted access,
regardless of if the request was authenticated or unauthenticated

This permission is not strictly required, since you can achieve the same result by using an empty list or tuple for the permissions setting, but you may find it useful to specify this class because it makes the intention explicit.

### IsAuthenticated¶ {#isauthenticated}

`IsAuthenticated`

This permission is suitable if you want your API to only be accessible to registered users.

This permission is suitable if you want your API to only be accessible to a subset of trusted administrators.

To do that we're going to need to create a custom permission.

In the snippets app, create a new file,
`permissions.py`


`fromrest_frameworkimportpermissionsclassIsOwnerOrReadOnly(permissions.BasePermission):"""Custom permission to only allow owners of an object to edit it."""defhas_object_permission(self,request,view,obj):# Read permissions are allowed to any request,# so we'll always allow GET, HEAD or OPTIONS requests.ifrequest.methodinpermissions.SAFE_METHODS:returnTrue# Write permissions are only allowed to the owner of the snippet.returnobj.owner==request.user`

`CharField`
,
`BooleanField`
etc...  The untyped
`ReadOnlyField`
is always read-only, and will be used for serialized representations, but will not be used for updating model instances when they are deserialized. We could have also used

user_input: I want clients to page through a huge, constantly-growing table efficiently and never see duplicates when rows are inserted mid-scroll. Which pagination style and what's the catch?
reference: CursorPagination: consistent, fixed-time paging that avoids duplicates even as rows are inserted, but it needs a unique, unchanging ordering and only allows forward/reverse navigation.
reference_contexts: Cursor based pagination requires that there is a unique, unchanging ordering of items in the result set.
This pagination style only presents forward and reverse controls, and does not allow the client to navigate to arbitrary positions.
With extremely large datasets pagination using offset-based pagination styles may become inefficient or unusable.
The default class to use for queryset pagination.
llm_response:
To page through a huge, constantly-growing table efficiently without seeing duplicates when rows are inserted, you should use **`CursorPagination`**.

### The Catch
`CursorPagination` is more complex than other schemes and comes with the following limitations:
* **No arbitrary navigation:** It only provides forward and reverse controls; you cannot navigate to arbitrary positions in the result set.
* **Ordering requirements:** It requires a unique, unchanging ordering of items. The ordering field must be:
    * A non-nullable value that can be coerced to a string.
    * Not a float (to avoid precision errors).
    * Indexed in the database.
    * Ideally a timestamp, slug, or other value set only once upon creation.
* **Configuration:** You must define the ordering you want the scheme to be applied against (the default is `"-created"`).
llm_references:
Provides a consistent pagination view. When used properly
`CursorPagination`
ensures that the client will never see the same item twice when paging through records, even when new items are being inserted by other clients during the pagination process.
Supports usage with very large datasets. With extremely large datasets pagination using offset-based pagination styles may become inefficient or unusable. Cursor based pagination schemes instead have fixed-time properties, and do not slow down as the dataset size increases.

#### Details and limitations¶ {#details-and-limitations}

Proper use of cursor based pagination requires a little attention to detail. You'll need to think about what ordering you want the scheme to be applied against. The default is to order by
`"-created"`
. This assumes that
there must be a 'created' timestamp field
on the model instances, and will present a "timeline" style paginated view, with the most recently added items first.

### CursorPagination¶ {#cursorpagination}

The cursor-based pagination presents an opaque "cursor" indicator that the client may use to page through the result set. This pagination style only presents forward and reverse controls, and does not allow the client to navigate to arbitrary positions.

Cursor based pagination requires that there is a unique, unchanging ordering of items in the result set. This ordering might typically be a creation timestamp on the records, as this presents a consistent ordering to paginate against.

Cursor based pagination is more complex than other schemes. It also requires that the result set presents a fixed ordering, and does not allow the client to arbitrarily index into the result set. However it does provide the following benefits:

The built-in styles currently all use links included as part of the content of the response. This style is more accessible when using the browsable API.

Pagination is only performed automatically if you're using the generic views or viewsets. If you're using a regular
`APIView`
, you'll need to call into the pagination API yourself to ensure you return a paginated response. See the source code for the
`mixins.ListModelMixin`
and
`generics.GenericAPIView`
classes for an example.

Pagination can be turned off by setting the pagination class to
`None`
.

## Setting the pagination style¶ {#setting-the-pagination-style}

The pagination style may be set globally, using the
`DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS`
and
`PAGE_SIZE`
setting keys. For example, to use the built-in limit/offset pagination, you would do something like this:


`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS':'rest_framework.pagination.LimitOffsetPagination','PAGE_SIZE':100}`

#### New pagination schemes.¶ {#new-pagination-schemes}

Until now, there has only been a single built-in pagination style in REST framework. We now have page, limit/offset and cursor based schemes included by default.

The cursor based pagination scheme is particularly smart, and is a better approach for clients iterating through large or frequently changing result sets. The scheme supports paging against non-unique indexes, by using both cursor and limit/offset information. It also allows for both forward and reverse cursor pagination. Much credit goes to David Cramer for
this blog post (https://cra.mr/2011/03/08/building-cursors-for-the-disqus-api)
on the subject.

#### Pagination controls in the browsable API.¶ {#pagination-controls-in-the-browsable-api}

Paginated results now include controls that render directly in the browsable API. If you're using the page or limit/offset style, then you'll see a page based control displayed in the browsable API:

### LimitOffsetPagination¶ {#limitoffsetpagination}

This pagination style mirrors the syntax used when looking up multiple database records. The client includes both a "limit" and an
"offset" query parameter. The limit indicates the maximum number of items to return, and is equivalent to the
`page_size`
in other styles. The offset indicates the starting position of the query in relation to the complete set of unpaginated items.

Request
:


`GET https://api.example.org/accounts/?limit=100&offset=400`


Response
:


`HTTP200OK{"count":1023,"next":"https://api.example.org/accounts/?limit=100&offset=500","previous":"https://api.example.org/accounts/?limit=100&offset=300","results":[…]}`


#### Setup¶ {#setup_1}

To enable the
`LimitOffsetPagination`
style globally, use the following configuration:


`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS':'rest_framework.pagination.LimitOffsetPagination'}`

Proper usage of cursor pagination should have an ordering field that satisfies the following:

Should be an unchanging value, such as a timestamp, slug, or other field that is only set once, on creation.
Should be unique, or nearly unique. Millisecond precision timestamps are a good example. This implementation of cursor pagination uses a smart "position plus offset" style that allows it to properly support not-strictly-unique values as the ordering.
Should be a non-nullable value that can be coerced to a string.
Should not be a float. Precision errors easily lead to incorrect results.
Hint: use decimals instead.
(If you already have a float field and must paginate on that, an
example CursorPagination subclass that uses decimals to limit precision is available here (https://gist.github.com/keturn/8bc88525a183fd41c73ffb729b8865be#file-fpcursorpagination-py)
.)
The field should have a database index.

`classCustomPagination(pagination.PageNumberPagination):defget_paginated_response(self,data):returnResponse({'links':{'next':self.get_next_link(),'previous':self.get_previous_link()},'count':self.page.paginator.count,'results':data})`


We'd then need to set up the custom class in our configuration:


`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS':'my_project.apps.core.pagination.CustomPagination','PAGE_SIZE':100}`


Note that if you care about how the ordering of keys is displayed in responses in the browsable API you might choose to use an
`OrderedDict`
when constructing the body of paginated responses, but this is optional.

### Using your custom pagination class¶ {#using-your-custom-pagination-class}

To have your custom pagination class be used by default, use the
`DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS`
setting:


`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS':'my_project.apps.core.pagination.LinkHeaderPagination','PAGE_SIZE':100}`

llm_response:
For a rich, declarative way to filter a list on multiple model fields via query parameters, the documentation recommends using **`django-filter`**.

### Recommended Approach: `django-filter`
This library integrates with DRF and allows you to specify a `FilterSet` class for advanced filtering requirements. It enables requests such as:
`http://example.com/api/products?category=clothing&in_stock=True`

To use it:
1. Define a `FilterSet` class for your model fields.
2. Use the `DjangoFilterBackend` class in your view.
3. Refer to the [django-filter documentation](https://django-filter.readthedocs.io/en/latest/index.html) and the [DRF integration guide](https://django-filter.readthedocs.io/en/latest/guide/rest_framework.html).

### Alternative Third-Party Packages
If you require different functionality, the documentation lists several other third-party packages that integrate with DRF:

*   **`django-rest-framework-filters`**: Works with `DjangoFilterBackend` to create filters across relationships or multiple lookup types for a field.
*   **`django-url-filter`**: Provides a way to filter data via human-friendly URLs and supports nested filtersets for related data.
*   **`drf-url-filters`**: Applies filters on `ModelViewSet` querysets and supports validation of incoming query parameters using the `Voluptuous` library.
*   **`dynamic-rest`**: Extends `ModelSerializer` and `ModelViewSet` to add API query parameters for filtering, sorting, and including/excluding fields and relationships.
*   **`drf-flex-fields`**: Extends `ModelSerializer` and `ModelViewSet` to dynamically set fields and expand primitive fields to nested models via URL parameters.

reference: Apply a UniqueTogetherValidator in the serializer's Meta.validators with the queryset and the field names that must be unique as a set; note it implicitly treats those fields as required.

llm_response:
To prevent a user from creating two records with the same combination of two fields, you should use the `UniqueTogetherValidator`.

This validator must be applied to the `Meta` class of your serializer. It requires two arguments:
*   `queryset`: The queryset against which uniqueness is enforced.
*   `fields`: A list or tuple of the field names that must form a unique set.

**Example implementation:**

```python
from rest_framework import serializers
from rest_framework.validators import UniqueTogetherValidator

class ExampleSerializer(serializers.Serializer):
    # ... fields ...

    class Meta:
        validators = [
            UniqueTogetherValidator(
                queryset=ToDoItem.objects.all(),
                fields=['list', 'position']
            )
        ]
```

**Important Note:** The `UniqueTogetherValidator` imposes an implicit constraint that all fields it applies to are treated as required, unless they have a `default` value.

llm_response:
To exercise your views like a client by hitting URLs with GET, POST, and PUT requests using JSON bodies, DRF provides the `RequestsClient` class.

This class allows you to write tests that interact with your service interface in an end-to-end fashion while running in-process.

### How to use `RequestsClient`
You can perform requests by passing fully qualified URLs to the client's methods. For example, to perform a POST request with a JSON body:

```python
from rest_framework.test import RequestsClient

client = RequestsClient()
response = client.post(
```

*   **Stricter interaction:** It is stricter than the standard Django test client, requiring that all interactions occur via the API. You should perform test setup and assertions using API calls rather than interacting with database models directly.
*   **URLs:** You must provide fully qualified URLs.

### Alternative
DRF also provides `APIRequestFactory`, which supports standard methods like `.get()`, `.post()`, and `.put()`. However, `APIRequestFactory` requires you to manually initialize the request using `DummyView().initialize_request(request)` to work with the REST framework's `Request` object and data handling.

user_input: When an unauthenticated request is rejected I sometimes get 401 and sometimes 403. What actually decides which one DRF returns?
reference: It hinges on whether the first/highest-priority authentication class uses a WWW-Authenticate header: if it does, an unauthenticated denial is 401 with that header; if not, it's 403. A request that authenticated but lacked permission is always 403.
reference_contexts: The first authentication class set on the view is used when determining the type of response .
The request was not successfully authenticated, and the highest priority authentication class does not use WWW-Authenticate headers.
HTTP 401 Unauthorized HTTP 403 Permission Denied HTTP 401 responses must always include a WWW-Authenticate header, that instructs the client how to authenticate.
Signature: AuthenticationFailed(detail=None, code=None) Raised when an incoming request includes incorrect authentication.
llm_response:
Whether DRF returns a 401 or 403 response for an unauthenticated request depends on the authentication scheme in use, specifically the highest priority (first) authentication class set on the view [1, 7].

The rules are as follows:

*   **403 Forbidden:** This is returned if the request was successfully authenticated but permission was denied [1]. If the request was not successfully authenticated, a 403 is returned if the highest priority authentication class does not use `WWW-Authenticate` headers [1]. This occurs if the `.authenticate_header()` method is not overridden in the authentication scheme [4].
*   **401 Unauthorized:** This is returned if the request was not successfully authenticated and the highest priority authentication class does use `WWW-Authenticate` headers [1]. This requires the authentication scheme to implement the `.authenticate_header(self, request)` method, which returns the string used for the `WWW-Authenticate` header [4].

In summary, the decision is determined by whether the first authentication class on the view implements `.authenticate_header()` [4, 7].

Signature:
`AuthenticationFailed(detail=None, code=None)`

Raised when an incoming request includes incorrect authentication.

By default this exception results in a response with the HTTP status code "401 Unauthenticated", but it may also result in a "403 Forbidden" response, depending on the authentication scheme in use.  See the
authentication documentation (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/authentication/)

### NotAuthenticated¶ {#notauthenticated}

Signature:
`NotAuthenticated(detail=None, code=None)`

Raised when an unauthenticated request fails the permission checks.

By default this exception results in a response with the HTTP status code "401 Unauthenticated", but it may also result in a "403 Forbidden" response, depending on the authentication scheme in use.  See the
authentication documentation (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/authentication/)
for more details.

If the request is unauthenticated the default value of
`request.user`

`request.auth`

depends on the authentication policy being used, but it may typically be an instance of the token that the request was authenticated against.

If the request is unauthenticated, or if no additional context is present, the default value of

### .authenticators¶ {#authenticators}

In some circumstances instead of returning
`None`
, you may want to raise an
`AuthenticationFailed`
exception from the
`.authenticate()`
method.

Typically the approach you should take is:

If authentication is not attempted, return
`None`
.  Any other authentication schemes also in use will still be checked.
If authentication is attempted but fails, raise an
`AuthenticationFailed`
exception.  An error response will be returned immediately, regardless of any permissions checks, and without checking any other authentication schemes.

You
may
also override the
`.authenticate_header(self, request)`
method.  If implemented, it should return a string that will be used as the value of the
`WWW-Authenticate`
header in a
`HTTP 401 Unauthorized`
response.

If the
`.authenticate_header()`
method is not overridden, the authentication scheme will return
`HTTP 403 Forbidden`
responses when an unauthenticated request is denied access.

## Unauthorized and Forbidden responses¶ {#unauthorized-and-forbidden-responses}

When an unauthenticated request is denied permission there are two different error codes that may be appropriate.

HTTP 401 Unauthorized (https://www.w3.org/Protocols/rfc2616/rfc2616-sec10.html#sec10.4.2)
HTTP 403 Permission Denied (https://www.w3.org/Protocols/rfc2616/rfc2616-sec10.html#sec10.4.4)

HTTP 401 responses must always include a
`WWW-Authenticate`
header, that instructs the client how to authenticate.  HTTP 403 responses do not include the
`WWW-Authenticate`
header.

`request.user`
will be a Django
`User`
instance.
`request.auth`
will be
`None`
.

Unauthenticated responses that are denied permission will result in an
`HTTP 403 Forbidden`
response.

`PUT`

`PATCH`

`POST`
or
`DELETE`
requests.  See the
Django CSRF documentation (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/howto/csrf/#using-csrf-protection-with-ajax)
for more details.

Warning
